title: Do, no, ao, pelo
description: Join de, em, a and por to the article, say his and her with dele and dela, and talk about countries and cities.

guide.summary: Portuguese glues the short prepositions de, em, a and por to the article that follows: de + o is do, em + a is na. These joined forms are not optional; learn the four sets and you can say of the, in the, to the and through the.

sections.title: De + the article: do, da, dos, das
sections.text: De means of or from. When the next word is o, a, os or as, de and the article become one word. It also gives the Portuguese for ’s: the teacher’s book is o livro da professora.
steps: Find the noun after de.
Take its article: o, a, os or as.
Put d in front of the article: do, da, dos, das.

examples.en: I am coming from the market.

watch: Never write de o or de a: the joined form is the only correct one.
Gostar, precisar and lembrar take de, so they often need do or da: gosto do filme.

sections.title: Em + the article: no, na, nos, nas
sections.text: Em covers in, on and at. Before an article it joins it and loses its e: em + o is no.
steps: Find the noun after em.
Take its article.
Put n in front of the article: no, na, nos, nas.

examples.en: The keys are on the table.
My mother works at the hospital.

watch: English uses in, on or at; Portuguese uses em for all three.
Do not confuse no (in the) with não (no, not).

sections.title: A + the article: ao, à, aos, às
sections.text: The preposition a (to) joins the article too. With a masculine noun it gives ao; with a feminine noun the two a’s merge into à, written with a grave accent. In Brazil people often say para instead: vou para a praia.
steps: Check that the verb takes a: ir a, chegar a.
Find the article of the noun.
Masculine gives ao or aos; feminine merges into à or às, with the grave accent.

examples.en: Tomorrow I am going to the beach.
We are going to the cinema.

watch: The grave accent on à is the only sign of the article: a praia without it is just the beach.
Vou para a praia is just as natural in Brazil, and chegar no is common in speech.

sections.title: Por + the article: pelo, pela, pelos, pelas
sections.text: Por means through, along, by or for (thanks for). Before an article it becomes pel-: por + o is pelo.
steps: Find the noun after por.
Take its article.
Replace por with pel and add the article: pelo, pela, pelos, pelas.
watch: Thanking for something takes por: obrigado pelo presente, never para.

sections.title: De + ele, ela: dele, dela, deles, delas
sections.text: De also joins the pronouns ele, ela, eles and elas. Placed after a noun, dele means his and dela means her. They follow the owner, not the thing owned. Brazilians use them because seu and sua usually mean your.
steps: Ask who the owner is: a man, a woman, or several people.
Pick dele, dela, deles or delas by the owner.
Put it after the noun, and keep the article before the noun: o carro dele.
watch: O irmão dela: the brother stays masculine, only the owner is a woman.
Sua casa in Brazil usually means your house, not her house.

sections.title: Em + um, uma: num, numa
sections.text: Em can also join the word for a: em + um gives num, em + uma gives numa. Unlike do, no or pelo, this join is optional: em um and em uma are correct too.
steps: Check that the meaning is a, not the.
Pick um or uma by the gender of the noun.
Join them to em if you like: num, numa.

examples.en: I live in a small house.

watch: Num ends in m, never n.
Numa casa is in a house; na casa is in the house.

sections.title: Countries and cities
sections.text: Most countries take an article, so em and de join it: no Brasil, da França. A few countries and most cities take none: em Portugal, de São Paulo. Some cities keep an article: o Rio, so do Rio.
steps: Ask whether the place takes an article: o Brasil, a França, but Portugal, São Paulo.
With an article, join it to em or de: no, na, do, da.
Without one, use plain em or de.
watch: Portugal never takes an article: em Portugal.
In Portugal people say em França; in Brazil it is na França.

steps: Find the noun after de and its article.
Join them: do, da, dos, das.
Find the noun after em and its article.
Join them: no, na, nos, nas.
Find the article of the noun after a.
Masculine: ao, aos. Feminine: à, às, with the grave accent.
Find the noun after por and its article.
Join them: pelo, pela, pelos, pelas.
Identify the owner: man, woman, or several.
Pick dele, dela, deles or delas and put it after the noun.
Check the meaning is a, not the.
Join em with um or uma: num, numa (em um is also fine).
Does the place take an article? Brasil and França do; Portugal and most cities do not.
Join the article to em or de, or use em or de alone.

exercises.instruction: Choose de joined to the article.
exercises.hint: Carro is one thing. Is it o carro or a carro?
exercises.feedback: De melts into the article of carro.
exercises.explanation: Carro is masculine singular (o carro), so de + o gives do: a porta do carro, the car door.

mistakes.why: That is de with the feminine article. Carro is masculine (o carro), so the feminine form does not match it.
That is the plural contraction, for several things. There is only one car here.

exercises.instruction: Choose de joined to the article.

mistakes.why: That is de with o, for one masculine thing. Músicas are several, and feminine.
Right gender, but singular. Músicas ends in -s: there are several songs.
Right number, wrong gender. A música is feminine, so the masculine plural does not fit.

exercises.instruction: Write de joined to the article.

exercises.explanation: A professora is feminine singular, so de + a becomes da: o livro da professora, the teacher’s book.

That is the masculine form. The teacher here is a professora, a woman, so the article is feminine.
The article is missing. A particular teacher is meant, so the article is there and fuses with de.

exercises.explanation: Ir a + a praia: the preposition a and the article a fuse into one a with a grave accent. In speech, Brazilians also say vou para a praia.

That is a + o, for a masculine noun. Praia is feminine (a praia).

The preposition and the article join into one word; they are not written apart.

exercises.instruction: Write a joined to the article.

alternatives.message: Right, and very common in Brazil: ela vai para a farmácia. The exercise practises the a form.

exercises.explanation: Ir a + a farmácia: the two a’s merge into one, written with a grave accent.

That is a + o, for masculine nouns. Farmácia is feminine (a farmácia).
The merged form takes the grave accent, which leans left, not the acute accent.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word for his.
